p.src: Meanwhile, the four pilgrims took to the highway. This truly was the Buddhist land of the West, quite unlike other places: they saw wondrous flowers and precious herbs, ancient cypresses and venerable pines; wherever they passed, every family practiced goodness and every household offered food to monks; at the foot of every mountain they met people cultivating the Way, and among the woods they saw travelers reciting sutras.

They saw a Daoist acolyte standing at an angle before the mountain gate, who called out in answer, “Can those approaching be the scripture pilgrims from the Eastern Land?” The elder quickly straightened his robes and raised his head to look. p.src: The Great Sage Sun recognized him and cried, “Master, this is the Great Immortal Golden Crown of the Jade Truth Temple at the foot of Vulture Peak. He has come to receive us.” Only then did Tripitaka understand, and he stepped forward to salute him. The Great Immortal smiled and said, “Only this year have you arrived, holy monk. The Bodhisattva Guanyin deceived me. Ten years ago, she received the Buddha’s golden decree and went to the Eastern Land in search of a scripture pilgrim, saying originally that you would reach me in two or three years. I waited year after year without the faintest news, never imagining that we would meet only this year.” Tripitaka pressed his palms together and said, “You have taken great pains on our behalf, Great Immortal. I am deeply grateful, deeply grateful.” The four pilgrims then led the horse and carried the luggage into the temple together. There they were each formally introduced to the Great Immortal. He at once ordered tea to be served and a vegetarian meal laid out. He also told the young acolytes to heat fragrant water so the holy monk might bathe before ascending to the Buddha’s land. p.src: After the master and disciples had bathed, evening stole upon them unnoticed, so they rested for the night at the Jade Truth Temple.

p.src: Early the next morning, the Tang Monk changed his clothes, donned his brocade cassock and Vairocana cap, took his ringed staff in hand, and entered the hall to bow farewell to the Great Immortal. The Great Immortal smiled and said, “Yesterday you were in rags; today you are resplendent. Seeing you thus, one knows you are truly a disciple of the Buddha.” Tripitaka bowed farewell and was about to depart. The Great Immortal said, “Wait. Let me escort you.” Pilgrim said, “There is no need for you to escort us. Old Sun knows the way.” The Great Immortal replied, “The road you know is the path through the clouds. The holy monk has not yet taken to the clouds and must travel by the proper road.” Pilgrim said, “That is quite true. Though Old Sun has been here several times, I have always come and gone by cloud and have never actually set foot upon this ground. Since there is a proper road, we must trouble you to escort us along it. My master’s desire to worship the Buddha is ardent, so please do not delay.” Smiling warmly, the Great Immortal took the Tang Monk by the hand and guided the future Candana Merit Buddha toward the gate of the Dharma. It turned out that this road did not lead out through the mountain gate; it ran from the temple’s central hall and through a rear gate. Pointing toward Vulture Peak, the Great Immortal said, “Holy monk, look there in the middle of the sky. The place wreathed in five-colored auspicious light and a thousand layers of blessed mist is lofty Spirit Vulture Peak, the sacred realm of the Buddha.” At the sight of it, the Tang Monk immediately bowed down. Pilgrim laughed and said, “Master, we have not yet reached the place for bowing. As the saying goes, ‘A mountain in sight will wear a horse out before you reach it.’ It is still a great distance from here; why bow already? If you bow all the way to the summit, how many times will you have to knock your head?” The Great Immortal said, “Holy monk, you, the Great Sage, Marshal Tianpeng, and the Curtain-Lifting General have now reached the blessed land and can see Vulture Peak. I shall return.” Tripitaka therefore bowed farewell and went on his way.

p.src: The Great Sage led the Tang Monk and the others onward, walking slowly and steadily as they ascended Vulture Peak. Before they had gone five or six li, they came upon a flowing river whose surging waves rushed and splashed with a murmuring roar. It was some eight or nine li wide, and there was no trace of anyone in any direction. Alarmed, Tripitaka said, “Wukong, we must have taken the wrong road. Could the Great Immortal have pointed us the wrong way? This river is so broad and so turbulent, and there is no boat in sight. How are we to cross?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “The way is not wrong. Do you not see a great bridge over there? Only by crossing that bridge can you attain the true fruit.” When the elder and the others drew nearer to look, they saw a plaque beside the bridge bearing the three characters “Cloud-Surpassing Ferry.” The bridge itself was nothing but a single log. p.src: What a Great Sage! He strode forward, leaped onto the single-log bridge, and, swaying from side to side, ran across in a moment. From the far bank he beckoned and called, “Come over! Come over!” The Tang Monk waved his hand in refusal. Bajie and Sha Monk bit their fingers and said, “Impossible, impossible, impossible!” Pilgrim ran back from the other side, seized Bajie, and said, “Idiot, follow me! Follow me!” Bajie threw himself flat on the ground and cried, “Slippery, slippery, slippery! I cannot cross. Spare me and let me ride wind and mist to the other side.” Pilgrim held him down and said, “What kind of place do you think this is, that you should be allowed to ride wind and mist? You must cross this bridge before you can become a Buddha.” Bajie said, “Brother, then I do not mind if I never become a Buddha. I truly cannot cross it.” The two of them tugged and pulled at each other in playful contention beside the bridge until Sha Monk went over to mediate, whereupon they finally let go.

p.src: Tripitaka looked back and suddenly saw a man poling a boat toward them from downstream, calling, “Come aboard! Come aboard!” Overjoyed, the elder said, “Disciples, stop fooling around. A ferryboat is coming over there.” The three sprang up and stood still, all gazing toward it. When the little boat came close, they saw that it was a bottomless boat. With his fiery eyes and golden pupils, Pilgrim had already recognized the Dipankara Buddha, also called Namo Precious Banner Radiant King Buddha. A ferryboat is coming over there.”

Seeing it, Tripitaka was again alarmed and said, “How can your broken, bottomless boat carry anyone across?”
The Buddha replied, “This boat of mine:

p.src: Great Sage Sun joined his palms and said in thanks, “We are grateful for your kindness in coming to ferry our master across. Master, get aboard. Though this boat has no bottom, it is steady; no wind or wave could overturn it.” The elder still hesitated in alarm, so the Pilgrim braced him by the arm and gave him a push. Unable to keep his footing, the master tumbled into the water, but the boatman promptly seized him and hauled him upright onto the boat. The master shook out his clothes, stamped the water from his shoes, and complained about the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim then brought Sandy and Eight Rules aboard, together with the horse and the luggage, and they all stood upon the gunwales. The Buddha pushed off with gentle force, and presently they saw a corpse drifting down from upstream. The elder was greatly startled at the sight. The Pilgrim laughed. “Do not be afraid, Master. That is none other than you.” Eight Rules also said, “It is you, it is you.” Clapping his hands, Sandy also cried, “It is you, it is you!” The boatman struck up a work chant and said, “That is you—joyous indeed, joyous indeed!” The three disciples joined their voices with his. The boatman poled onward, and before long they passed safely and steadily across the Immortal Ford of Cloud-Soaring. Only then did Tripitaka turn and lightly leap onto the farther shore. p.src: When the four pilgrims reached shore and looked back, the bottomless boat had vanished without a trace. Only then did the Pilgrim explain that the boatman was the Buddha who Receives and Guides Souls. Tripitaka at last understood; he quickly turned around and instead thanked his three disciples. The Pilgrim said, “There is no need for thanks on either side; we have supported one another. Through Master we gained deliverance, found a path by which to cultivate merit, and happily attained the true fruit; and through our protection, Master upheld the teaching with divine aid and joyfully cast off his mortal frame. Master, look at this wondrous realm before us, with its flowers and grasses, pines and bamboos, phoenixes, cranes, and deer. p.src: Master and disciples, carefree and at ease, walked to the summit of Spirit Mountain. Beneath the green pines they saw lay devotees arrayed, and amid the emerald cypresses, virtuous believers ranked in rows. The elder at once saluted them, causing the upasakas, upasikas, monks, and nuns hurriedly to join their palms and say, “Holy monk, do not salute us yet. After you have seen Shakyamuni, we may speak together.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Too soon, too soon! Let us first pay homage to the one in the highest seat.”

p.src: The elder could scarcely contain his joy; following the Pilgrim, he went straight to the outer gate of Thunderclap Monastery. There the Four Great Vajra Guardians came forward to receive him, asking, “Has the holy monk arrived?” Tripitaka bowed and replied, “Yes. This disciple Xuanzang has arrived.” Having answered, he made to enter the gate. The Vajra Guardian said, “Holy monk, wait a moment. Enter after we have reported your arrival.” One of the Vajra Guardians at the mountain gate went to notify the four guardians at the second gate, saying that the Tang monk had arrived; those at the second gate passed word to the third gate that the Tang monk had arrived. Within the third mountain gate were divine monks charged with preparing offerings. Hearing that the Tang monk had arrived, they hurried to the Hall of the Great Hero and reported to the Supreme Tathagata, Shakyamuni Buddha: “The holy monk of the Tang court has reached the precious mountain, come to obtain the scriptures.” The venerable Buddha was overjoyed. He immediately summoned the Eight Bodhisattvas, Four Vajra Guardians, five hundred arhats, three thousand guardians of the teaching, eleven great luminaries, and eighteen temple guardians, who formed two ordered ranks. Then he issued his golden command that the Tang monk be admitted. The command passed through every successive court within, all reverently obeying the Buddha’s decree and calling, “Let the holy monk enter.” The Tang monk, observing every rule and propriety, entered the mountain gate directly with Wukong, Wuneng, and Wujing, leading the horse and carrying the luggage. p.src: The four pilgrims came before the Hall of the Great Hero and prostrated themselves before the Tathagata. Afterward, they bowed again to those on the left and right. When each had completed three circuits, they knelt once more before the Buddha and respectfully presented their travel document. The Tathagata examined every part of it, then handed it back to Tripitaka. Tripitaka bowed his head in reverence and submitted, “This disciple Xuanzang, obeying the command of the Great Tang emperor in the Eastern Land, has journeyed from afar to this precious mountain to worshipfully seek the true scriptures and thereby save all living beings. May our Buddha bestow his grace and grant them swiftly, that we may return home.” The Tathagata then opened his compassionate lips and brought forth his merciful heart, saying to Tripitaka, “Your Eastern Land lies in Jambudvipa, the Southern Continent. Because its heaven is lofty, its earth abundant, its resources vast, and its people numerous, they are much given to greed and killing, lust and falsehood, deceit and fraud; they do not obey the Buddha’s teaching or turn toward wholesome affinities; they revere neither the Three Lights nor the Five Grains; they are neither loyal nor filial, neither righteous nor benevolent; they deceive their own consciences, use large measures in buying and small measures in selling, take lives, and slaughter animals. Thus they commit boundless wickedness and fill the measure of sin and evil, bringing upon themselves the calamities of hell. Therefore they fall forever into the nether darkness, endure all the torments of pounding and grinding, and are transformed into beasts. Many take forms covered in fur and crowned with horns, repaying their debts with their bodies and feeding men with their flesh. Those who fall forever into the Avici Hell and cannot ascend to deliverance do so for all these reasons. Though Master Kong established among them the teaching of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, and though successive emperors have governed with the penalties of exile, strangulation, and beheading, what can be done about those ignorant, unenlightened people who indulge themselves without restraint! I now possess a Tripitaka of scriptures that can deliver beings from anguish and absolve calamity and sin. Of these three collections, one is the Dharma collection, which discusses heaven; one is the Treatise collection, which speaks of earth; and one is the Sutra collection, which saves the dead. Together they comprise thirty-five divisions and a total of fifteen thousand one hundred and forty-four scrolls. They are truly the path to cultivating truth and the gate to upright goodness. Nothing concerning the astronomy, geography, peoples, birds and beasts, flowers and trees, implements, and human affairs of the world’s four great continents is left unrecorded. Since you have come from afar, I would give you the whole canon to take away. Yet the people of your land are foolish, coarse, and stubborn; they slander the true word and fail to comprehend the profound meaning of our Buddhist order.” He called, “Ananda and Kasyapa, lead these four pilgrims beneath the Treasure Pavilion and first serve them a vegetarian meal. After they have eaten, open the Precious Repository. From each of the thirty-five divisions of my Tripitaka, select several scrolls for them, so that they may spread them through the Eastern Land and forever pour forth this boundless grace.”

He called, “Ananda and Kasyapa, lead these four pilgrims beneath the Treasure Pavilion and first serve them a vegetarian meal.

u.src: After they have eaten, open the Precious Repository. From each of the thirty-five divisions of my Tripitaka, select several scrolls for them, so that they may spread them through the Eastern Land and forever pour forth this boundless grace.”

p.src: The two venerable disciples obeyed the Buddha’s command and led the four pilgrims beneath the pavilion. There was no end to the rare treasures and wondrous valuables arrayed there. They saw the deities charged with the offerings lay out a vegetarian banquet, all of it immortal delicacies, immortal dishes, immortal tea, and immortal fruits—a hundred exquisite flavors unlike anything in the mortal world. Master and disciples bowed in gratitude for the Buddha’s grace, then ate as much as they pleased. Truly:

p.src: Ānanda and Kāśyapa led the Tang Monk through the entire catalogue of scriptures, then said to him, “Holy monk, you have come here from the Eastern Land. What gifts have you brought us? Bring them out quickly, and we shall hand over the scriptures for you to take away.” Tripitaka replied, “This disciple Xuanzang has journeyed from very far away and prepared nothing.” The two venerable ones laughed. “Very well, very well! If scriptures are handed down to posterity for nothing, those who come after us will starve to death.” Seeing their coy insinuations and their refusal to hand over the scriptures, Pilgrim could contain himself no longer and shouted, “Master, let us go and complain to the Tathāgata! Have him come and give the scriptures to me himself!” Ānanda said, “Do not make such a din! What place do you think this is, that you still dare behave so outrageously? Come over here and receive the scriptures.” Bajie and Sha Monk mastered their tempers and restrained Pilgrim. Then they turned to receive the scriptures, packing the scrolls one by one into bundles. Some were loaded on the horse, while two more loads were tied up for Bajie and Sha Monk to carry. They returned before the jeweled throne, kowtowed in thanks to the Tathāgata, and went straight out through the gate. Whenever they passed a Buddha, they bowed twice; whenever they saw a bodhisattva, they bowed twice. At the main gate they bowed to the monks, nuns, laywomen, and laymen, bade each of them farewell, descended the mountain, and set out upon the road. Of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Now atop the jeweled pavilion sat the Ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara. From the pavilion he had quietly listened to the handing over of the scriptures and understood the matter perfectly: Ānanda and Kāśyapa had given them wordless scriptures. He smiled to himself and said, “The monks of the Eastern Land are deluded and cannot recognize the wordless scriptures. Would that not make the holy monk’s entire arduous journey a waste?” He asked, “Who is here beside my seat?” The Venerable White Hero stepped forward. The Ancient Buddha instructed him, “Exercise your divine power and fly like a shooting star to overtake the Tang Monk. Seize those wordless scriptures, so that he will return to ask for the true scriptures that bear writing.” The Venerable White Hero immediately mounted a violent wind, swept beyond the mountain gate of Thunderclap Monastery, and brought his divine power fully into play. What a wind it was! Truly:

p.src: As Elder Tang was traveling along, he suddenly heard a fragrant wind surging around him. Taking it for an auspicious sign from the Buddha, he was entirely unguarded. Then came a sudden noise, and a hand reached down from midair and lightly snatched away the scriptures borne by the horse. Tripitaka was so terrified that he beat his breast and cried out. Bajie tumbled along the ground in pursuit, Sha Monk guarded the loads of scriptures, and Sun Pilgrim sped after the thief as though in flight. When the Venerable White Hero saw Pilgrim drawing near, he feared that the cudgel had no eyes and might, in the heat of the moment, fail to distinguish friend from foe and injure him. He therefore tore the scripture bundle apart and flung it down into the dust. Seeing the bundle burst open and its contents scattered by the fragrant wind, Pilgrim lowered his cloud to attend to the scriptures and pursued no farther. The Venerable White Hero stilled the wind and gathered in the mist, then returned to report to the Ancient Buddha. Of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Bajie had gone in pursuit, but when he saw the books of scripture fall, he gathered them up with Pilgrim and carried them back to the Tang Monk. With tears streaming from his eyes, the Tang Monk said, “Disciples, even here in the World of Ultimate Bliss there are vicious demons who seek to harm us.” Sha Monk took the scattered scriptures they were carrying and opened one. It was pure white, without the slightest trace of writing. He hurriedly handed it to Tripitaka and said, “Master, there is no writing on this scroll.” Pilgrim opened another scroll and looked; it too was blank. Bajie opened one, and it too was blank. Tripitaka cried, “Open them all and see!” Every scroll was nothing but blank paper. Sighing again and again, the elder said, “The people of our Eastern Land are indeed without blessing. What use is there in taking back blank volumes such as these, with no writing in them? How could I dare face the Tang emperor? For the crime of deceiving my sovereign, even death would be insufficient punishment.” Pilgrim had already understood what had happened. He said to the Tang Monk, “Master, say no more. Those scoundrels Ānanda and Kāśyapa asked us for gifts, and because we had none, they gave us these books of blank paper. Let us hurry back and accuse them before the Tathāgata of extortion and fraud.” Bajie shouted, “Exactly, exactly! Let us go and accuse them!” The four travelers hurried back toward the mountain, their steps faltering in their haste, and swiftly climbed once more to Thunderclap Monastery.

p.src: Before long they reached the mountain gate, where everyone greeted them with folded hands and smiles, saying, “Has the holy monk come back to exchange the scriptures?” Tripitaka nodded and thanked them. The vajra guardians did not obstruct them, but let them pass straight to the Hall of the Great Hero. Pilgrim shouted, “Tathāgata! My master and we disciples have endured countless stings and demons, untold hardships and sufferings, and have bowed our way here from the Eastern Land. By your command the scriptures were to be handed over to us, but when Ānanda and Kāśyapa failed to extort gifts from us, they conspired together in fraud and deliberately made us take away blank books with no writing in them. What use are they to us? We beg the Tathāgata to punish them by decree.” The Buddha smiled and said, “Cease your shouting for the moment. I already know that the two of them asked you for gifts. But scriptures must not be lightly handed down, nor may they be obtained for nothing. Some time ago, when the holy monks among the bhikṣus descended the mountain, they recited these scriptures once at the home of Elder Zhao in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, ensuring safety for the living members of his household and deliverance for the dead. Yet they brought back only three pecks and three pints of grain-sized gold. Even then I said they had sold them far too cheaply, leaving their disciples and descendants without money to spend. Since you have now come empty-handed to obtain them, blank copies were handed to you. Those blank copies are the true wordless scriptures, and they are good in their own way. But because the beings of your Eastern Land are foolish, deluded, and unenlightened, only these written scriptures can be transmitted to them.” He then called out, “Ānanda, Kāśyapa! Quickly select several scrolls from each collection of the true scriptures that bear writing and give them to these travelers. Then come here and report the total.”

p.src: The two venerable ones once more led the four travelers beneath the precious towers and jeweled pavilions, where they again asked the Tang Monk for gifts. Tripitaka had nothing with which to oblige them, so he ordered Sha Monk to bring out the purple-gold alms bowl. Offering it in both hands, he said, “This disciple is truly poor, and the road was long, so I prepared no gifts. This alms bowl was bestowed upon me by the Tang emperor with his own hands, that I might use it to beg for food along the road. Today I offer it to you as a small token of my sincerity. I earnestly beg the venerable ones to accept it. When I return to court and report to the Tang emperor, he will surely reward you handsomely. I ask only that you bestow upon us the true scriptures that bear writing, so that the purpose of this imperial mission and the toil of our distant journey may not be in vain.” Ānanda accepted it with only a faint smile. The strongmen who guarded the precious towers, the cooks in charge of the fragrant kitchens, and the venerable ones who watched over the pavilions crowded around—one wiping his face, another slapping his back, some snapping their fingers and others twisting their lips—and laughed one after another, saying, “Shameless, shameless! Demanding a gift from those who came for the scriptures!” In a moment his face was wrinkled with shame, yet he still clung to the alms bowl and would not let it go. Only then did Kāśyapa enter the pavilion to select the scriptures, checking them one by one before handing them to Tripitaka. Tripitaka called out, “Disciples, inspect them all carefully. Do not let it be as it was before.” The three disciples took each scroll and examined it, and every one bore writing. They were given five thousand and forty-eight scrolls, the number of one complete canon. They packed them all in good order and loaded them onto the horse; what remained filled another load, which Bajie shouldered. Sha Monk carried their own baggage. Pilgrim led the horse, and the Tang Monk took up his priest’s staff, straightened his Vairocana cap, and shook out his brocade cassock. Only then did they joyfully return before our Buddha, the Tathāgata. Indeed:

The Tathāgata ascended high upon his lotus throne and ordered the two great arhats, Dragon-Subduer and Tiger-Tamer, to sound the cloud chime and summon from every quarter the three thousand Buddhas, the three thousand Jiedi guardians, the Eight Vajra Guardians, the Four Bodhisattvas, the five hundred venerable arhats, the eight hundred bhikṣus, the assembled upāsakas, bhikṣuṇīs, and upāsikās, and all venerable ones and holy monks, great and small, from every heaven and cave dwelling, every blessed land and sacred mountain. p.src: Tripitaka and his three disciples tethered the horse and set down their loads; each joined his palms, bowed, and paid homage toward the throne. The Tathāgata said to the Tang monk, “The merit and virtue of these scriptures are beyond measure. Though they are the mirror and exemplar of our school, they are in truth the wellspring of the Three Teachings. When you reach your Southern Jambudvīpa, show them to all living beings, and do not permit them to be treated lightly or with disrespect. No one may open a scroll without first bathing and observing purification. Treasure them and hold them in reverence. For within them lie the profound mysteries by which one may become an immortal and attain the Way, and the wondrous methods that illuminate the myriad transformations of creation.” Tripitaka bowed his head to the ground and gave thanks for the grace bestowed, accepting the teachings in faith and vowing to carry them out. Once more, he and his companions made three full rounds of obeisance to the Buddha, humbly pledged their sincere devotion, received the scriptures, and departed. When they reached the three mountain gates, they thanked all the holy ones in turn; of this, no more need be said.

p.src: Only after the Tang monk had been sent on his way did the Tathāgata dismiss the assembly for the transmission of the scriptures. Then Guanyin Bodhisattva stepped forward from the side, joined her palms, and addressed the Buddha: “Years ago, your disciple received the golden decree and went to the Eastern Land to seek one who would obtain the scriptures. The undertaking has now succeeded. In all, it has taken fourteen years, or five thousand and forty days—still eight days short, and thus not in accord with the number of scrolls in the canon. I beseech the World-Honored One to grant that the holy monk return east and then come back west without delay, so that within eight days the number of the canon may be completed. Then permit your disciple to return the golden decree.” The Tathāgata was greatly delighted and said, “What you say is entirely fitting. You may return the golden decree.” He immediately summoned the Eight Great Vajra Guardians and instructed them: “Quickly exert your divine power and escort the holy monk back to the East. Once the true scriptures have been transmitted and preserved there, bring the holy monk back to the West. You must accomplish this within eight days, thereby completing the number of the canon. Do not delay or disobey.” The Vajra Guardians at once caught up with the Tang monk and called, “Scripture pilgrims, follow us!” The Tang monk and his companions all felt light of body and strong of limb; drifting freely through the air, they followed the Vajra Guardians and rose upon the clouds. And so it was that:
